title: Johns Hopkins trial finds that a fully automated AI diabetes prevention program matched human coaching and reached more people
summary: In a 368-person Johns Hopkins trial, the *Sweetch* AI-led diabetes prevention program met the risk-reduction goal as often as human coaching (31.7% vs 31.9%).
account: Researchers at Johns Hopkins Medicine ran a randomized noninferiority trial from 11 October 2021 to 16 December 2024 at sites in Baltimore, Maryland, and Reading, Pennsylvania. They referred 368 adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity either to an AI-led diabetes prevention program from Sweetch Health or to one of four human-led programs recognized by the CDC. The Sweetch app used a reinforcement learning algorithm to time and tailor push messages on weight, activity and food. After 12 months, 31.7% of the AI group and 31.9% of the human-coaching group met the combined goal for weight loss, physical activity or HbA1c reduction. That result met the prespecified noninferiority margin. More people started the AI program (93.4% against 82.7%) and more completed it (63.9% against 50.3%). The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases funded the trial. Sweetch was paid to deliver the program and took no part in the analysis. The human programs ran remotely because of COVID-19, and the trial measured risk factors in place of new cases of diabetes.
purpose: The Sweetch program was built to deliver the Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle intervention without human coaches. The measured benefit is that purpose.
